stem: Which goat breed is a white dairy breed with a high milk yield?

options.content: Saanen
options.rationale: Correct: a Swiss dairy breed.

options.content: Boer goat
options.rationale: A meat breed with a white body and red-brown head.

options.content: Angora
options.rationale: Kept for mohair.

options.content: Kalahari Red
options.rationale: A red-brown meat breed.

explanation: The Saanen is the main exotic dairy goat.

stem: Which of these is an indigenous sheep breed of Zimbabwe?

options.content: Sabi
options.rationale: Correct: a hardy, fat-tailed hair sheep.

options.content: Dorper
options.rationale: An exotic meat breed developed in South Africa.

options.content: Merino
options.rationale: An exotic fine-wool breed.

options.content: Boer
options.rationale: The Boer is a goat breed.

explanation: The Sabi is indigenous; the Dorper and Merino are exotic.

stem: How does the feeding behaviour of goats differ from that of sheep?

options.content: Goats graze grass close to the ground; sheep browse trees
options.rationale: This is the wrong way round.

options.content: Goats and sheep eat exactly the same plants in the same way
options.rationale: Their preferences differ, which is why mixed flocks use veld well.

options.content: Goats eat only concentrates and cannot digest leaves
options.rationale: Goats are ruminants that digest leaves well.

options.content: Goats mainly browse shrubs and trees; sheep graze close to the ground
options.rationale: Correct.

explanation: Goats are browsers and sheep are grazers, so they compete little.

stem: Why is a raised slatted floor recommended in a goat house?

options.content: It lets the goats see predators approaching at night
options.rationale: This is not the reason.

options.content: It makes the house warmer in the rainy season
options.rationale: A raised floor is cooler and drier, not warmer.

options.content: Droppings fall through and the floor stays dry, reducing foot rot and worms
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: It allows the farmer to keep twice as many goats in the same small house
options.rationale: Stocking density must still be reasonable.

explanation: A dry, clean floor reduces pneumonia, foot rot and worm infection.
hints: What happens to droppings and urine on a slatted floor?

stem: A farmer wants more twins from her does next season. What should she do?

options.content: Reduce their feed so they become lean before mating
options.rationale: Poor condition lowers ovulation and conception.

options.content: Feed the does better for 2-3 weeks before and during mating
options.rationale: Correct: flushing raises the ovulation rate.

options.content: Keep the buck with the does all year round
options.rationale: This spreads kidding but does not cause twins.

options.content: Mate the does as soon as they are weaned at about three months old
options.rationale: They are far too young.

explanation: Flushing increases the number of eggs released, so more does have twins.
hints: What raises the number of eggs released?

stem: Several goats are weak, with pale inner eyelids and swelling under the jaw. Which problem is most likely?

options.content: Foot rot
options.rationale: Foot rot causes lameness and a foul smell from the hooves.

options.content: Wireworm infection causing anaemia
options.rationale: Correct: these worms suck blood in the abomasum.

options.content: Heartwater
options.rationale: Heartwater is tick-borne and causes nervous signs and fever.

options.content: Overfeeding during flushing, which makes the goats fat and slow
options.rationale: Overfeeding does not cause pale eyelids.

explanation: Pale membranes (anaemia) and bottle jaw are classic signs of wireworm; dose and improve grazing management.

stem: A farmer with local Mashona does wants faster-growing kids without losing hardiness. What is the best plan?

options.content: Replace all the does with Saanen does
options.rationale: Saanens are dairy goats needing good feed and shelter.

options.content: Keep only Mashona bucks and does and feed them less
options.rationale: This will not raise growth rate.

options.content: Mate the local does with a Boer buck
options.rationale: Correct: crossbred kids grow faster and keep much of the dam's hardiness.

options.content: Buy Merino rams to mate with the does to improve their growth rate
options.rationale: Rams cannot breed with goats.

explanation: Crossbreeding with a meat breed such as the Boer improves growth while the local dam provides hardiness and mothering ability.

stem: The gestation period of both goats and sheep is about 150 days.
A kidding percentage of 140% must be a mistake, because a percentage cannot be more than 100.
explanation: False. Kids born ÷ does mated × 100 exceeds 100% when twins are common.

stem: Match each management practice with its reason.

right.content: Controls wireworm and other internal parasites

explanation: Each routine practice protects health or production.

stem: Name the tick-borne disease of goats and sheep spread by the bont tick.
explanation: **Heartwater** is spread by the bont tick; goats and sheep are very susceptible.

stem: 30 ewes were mated and 39 lambs were born. Calculate the lambing percentage.
A Dorper lamb weighed 4 kg at birth and 28 kg at 150 days. Calculate its average daily gain, in kg/day.
Describe a suitable house for a flock of goats.

points.description: Raised slatted floor about a metre off the ground so droppings fall through and the floor stays dry.
Roof and walls that keep out rain and wind but allow ventilation.
Secure doors/walls against predators and thieves.
Feed racks above floor level, water troughs and separate pens for kids and the buck.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The house should have a raised slatted floor, a roof and walls that keep out rain and draughts while allowing ventilation, strong lockable doors against predators and thieves, and raised feed racks, water troughs and separate pens for kids and the buck.

stem:
A farmer near Gokwe kept these records for her goat flock. In season 2 she flushed the does before mating.

| Season | Does mated | Does that kidded | Kids born | Kids weaned |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Season 1 (no flushing) | 50 | 44 | 55 | 46 |
| Season 2 (flushed) | 50 | 46 | 74 | 64 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the kidding percentage in season 1.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the weaning percentage in season 2.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain how flushing caused the change in the number of kids born.

points.description: Better feeding before and during mating raised the does' body condition.
So more eggs were released (higher ovulation rate) and more does had twins: kids born rose from 55 to 74.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: In season 2, 10 of the 74 kids died before weaning. Suggest **three** ways to reduce these losses.

points.description: Ensure every kid gets colostrum soon after birth, especially twins (help weak kids to suck).
Keep does and kids in a dry, sheltered, predator-proof pen; dip navels.
Feed does well in late pregnancy and lactation; creep-feed kids; control worms and ticks.

explanation: Calculate flock performance and explain the effect of flushing.

stem:
After a wet season, a farmer checked the colour of the inner eyelids of 50 goats (red is healthy; white is severe anaemia).

| Colour of the inner eyelid | Number of goats |
| --- | --- |
| Red | 22 |
| Pink | 15 |
| Pale pink | 8 |
| White | 5 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage of goats with pale pink or white eyelids.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Name the blood-sucking internal parasite most likely to be causing the anaemia.
parts.explanation: Wireworm (*Haemonchus*) sucks blood in the abomasum.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why worm problems are worst after a wet season.

points.description: Worm eggs and larvae on the pasture survive and develop best in warm, moist conditions.
Goats grazing wet, short grass pick up many larvae.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest **three** ways to control worms in the flock.

points.description: Dose the anaemic goats (and the flock at strategic times) with an approved dewormer at the correct dose.
Rotate grazing/move goats to clean paddocks; let goats browse rather than graze short wet grass.
House on raised slatted floors, keep feed off the ground, and cull goats that are repeatedly anaemic.

parts.explanation: Dosing, grazing management, hygiene and selection.

explanation: Interpret eyelid colour scores for anaemia and plan worm control.
hints: Pale pink and white show anaemia.
